comments.author: throwaway275275275
comments.body: Does it only do generation of a full game from nothing or can it work on an existing game for iteration/improvement/feedback ? Like if you want to add a feature to a game that was already generated for example

replies.author: crush-name
replies.body:
Right now it works best on projects it generated itself — the pipeline knows the structure it created, so iterating on those (adding features, tweaking mechanics, fixing issues) is already supported.
For arbitrary Godot projects it'd be more limited — mostly useful as a GDScript programming assistant rather than a full creative partner, since it wouldn't have the same context about the project's architecture.

comments.author: ActionFlash
comments.body: Honest question...what is the point of this? I'm not against using AI for certain tasks, but why use it to create EVERYTHING? On the Github page it states "no human in the loop", why would you want to a play a game that no human has had a hand in creating?

replies.author: crush-name
replies.body:
Great question! The "no human in the loop" framing is about proving the concept — can AI handle the full pipeline end-to-end? That's the technical challenge I've been focused on.
But the end vision is really a developer partner that takes the boring parts off your plate. You describe what you want in natural language, see it running, then guide it iteratively. The human is very much in the loop — just at the creative level instead of wrestling with boilerplate and engine quirks.
Good point on the description though, I'll adjust it to reflect that better. Thanks!

replies.author: Aeshulli
replies.body:
How about for anyone with literally zero experience or expertise in game development? Being able to simply have an idea and actually get a playable game sounds like a pretty magical, wonderful thing for a lot of people. There are far more players of games out there than maker of games.

And speaking personally as a woman, I've been gaming for decades wishing all sorts of games existed. But this industry has largely ignored the massive demand for games specifically catering to women. Even though women now comprise 50% of gamers, they're very much still not well-represented in the development pipeline so there are huge niches just begging to be filled (and absolute heaps of cash left sitting on the table because of it). Reducing the barrier to entry in creating games with AI is incredibly exciting.

replies.author: ActionFlash
replies.body: I agree with you on every point you made, except one. I don't agree that a tool that completely creates a game for you really helps at all, because it's never going to be exactly what you want, as you have so little control. I'm all for using whatever tools are available to get your game made, but not completely removing the human element, which is what this tool does. It's amazing from a technical stand point, but I think there are better ways to achieve what you'd like.

comments.author: DamnageBeats
comments.body:
So, I downloaded your repo and have been tinkering with it a whole bunch. I got it to run on Kimi 2.5 with a little work. I am working on making sure it runs with all common LLMs as well as local ones as well.

I have added, not yet tested, a bunch more presets, the ability to use your own assets, including sprites, music, and story script. (I believe the local sprite and music is working).

The biggest thing I did was give it a webUI. Now instead of running it in a cli or ide you can simply run it in your browser, see everything easily and know what’s going on at all times. I added progress bars for individual file creation.

I also fixed a few things, like pause/resume. It was stuck as a UI only implementation, it wasn’t actually doing anything in the back-end.

I also added the ability to add-on to and extend games.

I added the ability to save different systems we create as “assets” so they can be reused, so the LLM doesn’t always have to rewrite entire systems it already made.

I got a ton of ideas I want to add to it as well.

1. Instead of making a “full 1-shot game” let it craft small portions, like one stage or dungeon or even character or monster or whatever at a time.
2. I found an old school final fantasy style music generator I want to embed into this as well.
3. Right now I added sprites and stuff I bought for rpgmaker mz, and added it to the pipeline. Seems to work

Here is an image of the home page, pre a bunch of new work.

You still have full control if its public. You can allow others to submit change requests (pull requests) or disable it whatsoever being a sole contributor. 

Most importantly, make sure you are not sharing any private information in your files.

Don't feel noobish, i'd say being cautious around things you have little experience in is  smart. Justvkeep moving at your pace and you're good. This git stuff can appear daunting, but once you get your feet wet, it's not too bad.

I don’t have one, and am not paying for one right now, so I cannot fully test that portion of the pipeline, although, the demo is showing it works, so I am assuming the original creator had an account and tested it. 

I’m still doing testing. Just trying not to kill my api quotas. I’m already at my limit for the week on gpt, so I can’t try that pipeline yet. I did get a basic asteroids game working, but that baseball game I tried needs either the tripo3d account or sprites for the game. 

Next I am going for a metroidvania, with my provided sprites. I’ll post results.
